en: (Madhyamaka-śālistamba-sūtra) / Homage to the Buddha!
Neither ceasing nor arising, neither annihilated nor eternal,
not a unity nor a plurality, without coming and without going.
I pay homage to the Fully Awakened One, the best among speakers, who taught dependent origination— the auspicious stilling of conceptual proliferation.
Why is it called "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*)? It is said to have causes and conditions, not to be without cause or without condition.
Furthermore, this dependent origination arises from two reasons.
By which two causes does it arise?
By way of causal connection (*hetūpanibandha*) and by way of conditional connection (*pratyayopanibandha*).
That too should be understood as twofold: external (*bāhya*) and internal (*ādhyātmika*).
In that regard, what is the causal connection of external dependent origination?
It is as follows: from the seed comes the sprout;
from the sprout, the leaf.
From the leaf comes the stalk; from the stalk, the node; from the node, the stem.
From the stalk comes the embryo; from the embryo, the awn; from the awn, the flower.
"From the flower comes the fruit":
when the seed is absent, the sprout does not arise; likewise, up to the point that when the flower is absent, the fruit does not arise.
But when the seed exists, the production of the sprout occurs; likewise, up to the point that when the flower exists, the production of the fruit occurs.
And yet, in that process, it does not occur to the seed: "I am producing the sprout."
By this, [their] lack of agency is shown:
it does not occur to the sprout, "I am produced by the seed"; and likewise, up to the flower, it does not occur, "I am producing the fruit."
Nor does it occur to the fruit: "I have been produced by the flower.
Rather, when the seed exists as the cause, the production and manifestation of the sprout occurs; and so on, until, when the flower exists, the production and manifestation of the fruit occurs.
And in this way, the causal connection of external dependent origination is to be understood.
Furthermore, how is the conditional dependence of external dependent origination to be viewed? It is through the conjunction of the six elements (*dhātu*).
An element is so called because it maintains its own nature (*svabhāva*).
From the conjunction of which six elements?
That is to say, the conditional dependence of external dependent origination should be seen as resulting from the combination of the earth, water, fire, air, and space elements.
Among these, the earth element performs the function of supporting the seed.
The water element moistens the seed;
the fire element ripens the seed;
the wind element brings forth the seed.
The space element performs the function of non-obstruction for the seed,
and the season also performs the function of transformation for the seed.
In the absence of these conditions, the production of the sprout from the seed does not occur.
When the external earth element is unimpaired,
and likewise the water, fire, wind, space, and season elements are unimpaired,
then from the conjunction of all these, as the seed ceases, the production of the sprout occurs.
In that regard, it does not occur to the earth element, "I perform the function of supporting the seed.
Likewise, up to and including the season, it does not occur, "I perform the function of transforming the seed.
Nor does it occur to the sprout, "I am produced by these conditions."
Furthermore, when those conditions are present, as the seed ceases, the production of the sprout occurs.

And this sprout is not self-made, not made by another, not made by both, not created by a Lord (Īśvara), not transformed by time, not arisen from primordial nature (prakṛti), not dependent on no cause, nor is it produced without a cause;
rather, through the conjunction of the elements of earth, water, fire, air, and space, as the seed ceases, the production of the sprout occurs.
In this way, the conditional dependence of external dependent origination is to be understood.
In this regard, external dependent origination is to be viewed through five reasons.
Which five?
Not as eternal, not as annihilated, not as transmigrating, from a small cause there is the production of a vast fruit, and there is a continuous succession of similar [states].
How is it not eternal?
Because the sprout is one thing and the seed is another; it is not the case that the seed itself is the sprout.
Moreover, the seed ceases and the sprout arises;
therefore, it is not eternal.
How, then, is it not from annihilation? A sprout is not produced from a seed that has already ceased,
nor is it produced from a seed that has not ceased.
Moreover, the seed ceases and at that very same moment the sprout arises,
like the rising and falling of the ends of a balance scale.
Therefore, it is not from annihilation.
How is it not by way of transmigration? Because the sprout is dissimilar to the seed, it is therefore not by way of transmigration.
How is it that from a small cause there is the production of a vast fruit?
A small seed is sown (because of its pervasiveness— [not] non-pervasive)—
it brings about a vast fruit.
Therefore, from this small cause, there arises a vast fruit.
How is it "by way of a continuous succession similar to that"?
Just as whatever kind of seed is sown, such a kind of fruit is produced; therefore, it is said to be "by way of a continuous succession similar to that."
Thus, external dependent origination is to be viewed through five reasons.
Furthermore, therein, what is the causal connection (*hetūpanibandha*) of internal dependent origination?
It is this: conditioned by ignorance are the formative forces (*saṃskāra*), up to: conditioned by birth are aging and death.
If ignorance did not exist, formative forces would not be perceived in this way.
And so on, up to: if birth did not exist—the manifestation of the five aggregates is what is called birth—[then aging and death would not be perceived].
In that state, old age and death will not be discerned;
yet, when ignorance exists, the production of the formative forces occurs.
In this regard, it does not occur to ignorance: "I am producing the formative forces."
Furthermore, it does not occur to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) that "we have been produced by ignorance.
Likewise, up to birth (*jāti*, the manifestation of the aggregates),
it does not occur that "I produce old age and death."
Even for aging and death, it does not occur thus: "I have been brought about by birth.
Nevertheless, when ignorance exists, there is the production and manifestation of the formative forces;
and so on, until when birth exists, there is the production and manifestation of aging and death.
In this way, the causal connection of internal dependent origination is to be observed.
Furthermore, how is the conditional dependence of internal dependent origination to be viewed?
It should be viewed as the coming together of the elements of earth, water, fire, air, space, and consciousness. In that regard, what is the earth element of internal dependent origination?
That which, through the cohesion (contact) of the body,
brings about the state of solidity—
this is called the earth element.
Furthermore, that which performs the function of grasping (or the function of appropriation and accumulation) for the body is called the water element.
Furthermore, that which digests what has been eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted by the body is called the fire element (tejodhātu).
That which performs the function of inhalation and exhalation for the body— [inhalation being the drawing in of air,
and this being its function]— is called the wind element.
That which produces the state of internal hollowness within the body is called the space element (ākāśadhātu).

That which brings about name-and-form (nāmarūpa) through the conjunction of a bundle of reeds— namely, the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) associated with the fivefold collection of consciousnesses (vijñānakāya), such as the visual consciousness, and accompanied by outflows (sāsrava) or obscurations (sāvaraṇa).
This is called the consciousness element.
In the absence of these conditions, the arising of the body does not occur.
And when the internal earth element is unimpaired, and likewise the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements are unimpaired, [the body arises].
Through the coming together of all these elements, the production of the body occurs.
In this regard, it does not occur to the earth element, "I am producing the solidity of the body.
Nor does it occur to the water element, "I am performing the function of cohesion for the body."
The fire element does not think: "I digest what has been eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted by the body.
The wind element does not think: "I perform the function of inhalation and exhalation for the body.
The space element does not think: "I produce the state of internal hollowness for the body."
The consciousness element does not think, "I bring about the body," nor does the body think, "I am produced by these specific conditions."
And yet, when the conditions are present, the arising of the body occurs.
In that regard, the earth element is not a self (neither liberated nor bound),
nor a living being, nor a creature, nor a human, nor a person, nor a woman, nor a man, nor a neuter; it is neither "I" nor "mine," nor does it belong to anyone else whatsoever.
Thus, the water element, the fire element, the wind element, the space element, and the consciousness element are not the self, nor do they belong to anything else whatsoever.
In this context, what is ignorance (*avidyā*)?

It is the various forms of non-knowing regarding these very six elements (*ṣaḍdhātu*), such as the notion of unity, the notion of a whole, the notion of permanence, the notion of stability, the notion of eternity, the notion of pleasure, and the notions of a sentient being, a living soul, a creature, a nourisher, a person, an individual, a human, or a descendant of Manu, and so forth.
This is called ignorance (*avidyā*).
When ignorance exists in this way, attachment, aversion, and delusion arise toward sense objects.
Among these, those which are attachment, aversion, and delusion toward sense objects—
These are called the formative forces (saṃskāra).
The designation of the object (consisting of the sense faculties, consciousness, and volition) is consciousness.
The four aggregates of clinging that arise simultaneously with consciousness are "name-and-form" (nāmarūpa).
The sense faculties based upon name-and-form are the "sixfold base" (ṣaḍāyatana).
The coming together of the three factors is contact (*sparśa*)— meaning the conjunction of the object, the sense faculty, and consciousness.
Feeling (*vedanā*) is the experience of that contact.

Craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is the attachment (*adhyavasāna*) to feeling—attachment being the longing [and] the experience of pleasure and so forth. Grasping (*upādāna*) is the intensification of craving. Existence (*bhava*) is the karma born from grasping that produces renewed existence.
Birth is the manifestation of the aggregates caused by existence;
aging is the maturation of the aggregates (meaning the decay of the aggregates);
death is the destruction of the aggregates.
Sorrow (*śoka*) is the internal burning of a deluded person who is dying and possessed of attachment.
Lamentation (*paridevana*) is the verbal expression resulting from that sorrow.
Suffering (*duḥkha*) is the unpleasant persistence associated with the five groups of sensory consciousness, such as the eye-consciousness, which consists of the remorse of suffering.
Mental suffering and dejection associated with attention,
as well as other such afflictions;

The secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) and distresses (*upāyāsa*)—namely, all those such as the delusion born of mental conceptualization, deceit, guile, despondency, sensual desire, and so forth—[are likewise included]. [The rest is as before.]

Furthermore—non-comprehension of reality, false comprehension, and ignorance [ignorance being the lack of knowledge regarding the distinction between the conventional and the ultimate] constitute ignorance (*avidyā*).

When ignorance exists, three kinds of formative forces (*saṃskāra*) are produced: those leading to merit, those leading to demerit, and those leading to the imperturbable; thus it is established that "formative forces have ignorance as their condition.
For formative forces leading to merit, there arises consciousness leading to merit.
For volitional formations leading to demerit, consciousness leads only to demerit; for volitional formations leading to the imperturbable, consciousness leads only to the imperturbable.
This is called "consciousness conditioned by volitional formations."
Thus, in this way, name-and-form has consciousness as its condition.
Through the growth of name-and-form, functional activities proceed by way of the six sense-bases;
therefore, that which is conditioned by name-and-form is called the six sense-bases.
From the six sense bases, the six groups of contact arise;
this is called contact conditioned by the six sense bases.
Whatever kind of contact occurs, a feeling of that same kind arises;
this is called "feeling conditioned by contact."
He who experiences that feeling, specifically relishes it, rejoices in it, becomes attached to it, and craves it.
It persists; that is called craving conditioned by feeling.
Relishing and rejoicing is the state of attachment; it is the thought,
"May I not be separated from these five strands of sensual pleasure that are dear and pleasant to me," and the repeated longing for them.
This is called "clinging conditioned by craving."
Praying in this way, one further arouses karma that produces renewed existence through body, mind, or speech; this is called "existence" (bhava) conditioned by grasping (upādāna).
The manifestation of the aggregates produced by karma is called birth conditioned by becoming.
The destruction that occurs through the accumulation and maturation of the aggregates produced by birth—

this is called "aging and death conditioned by birth. (As for the intermediate sections, therein grief, lamentation, suffering, dejection, and despair are indicated by way of abbreviation within the context of ignorance and the other links.)
In this context, consciousness is the cause by virtue of having the nature of a seed;
karma is the cause by virtue of having the nature of a field;
and ignorance and craving are the causes by virtue of having the nature of afflictions.
Karma and the afflictions produce the seed of consciousness.
In this process, karma performs the function of the field for the seed of consciousness,
while craving moistens the seed of consciousness.
Ignorance sows the seed of consciousness;
through these existing conditions, the production of the seed of consciousness occurs.
In this regard, it does not occur to karma: "I am performing the function of the field for the seed of consciousness."
Craving also does not think, "I moisten the seed of consciousness. Ignorance also does not think, "I cast down the seed of consciousness.
The seed of consciousness also does not think, "I am [produced] by these conditions (dependent originations)."
It is said to be "produced."
Rather, the seed of consciousness, established in the field of karma, moistened by the moisture of craving, and covered with the soil of ignorance, sprouts;
thus the production of the sprout of name-and-form occurs.

And that sprout of name-and-form is not self-made, not made by another, not made by both, not created by a Lord, not transformed by time, not produced from primordial matter (*prakṛti*), not dependent on no cause, nor is it arisen without a cause; rather, through the union of mother and father, the convergence of the season, and the assembly of other conditions, the seed of consciousness— awakened by craving— brings about the sprout of name-and-form there in the mother’s womb by way of rebirth.

In phenomena that are ownerless (due to the selflessness of dharmas), devoid of a self (due to the selflessness of persons), without "mine," without possession, without adversaries, equal to space, and having the nature of an illusory object;
Because there is no deficiency in causes and conditions. (The term *peyālam*—by which word he indicates that the explanation is incomplete—is used.)
For example, visual consciousness arises through five causes. What are these five?
Dependent upon the eye, forms, light, space, and the attention arising therefrom, visual consciousness arises.
In that regard, the eye performs the function of being the basis for visual consciousness;
visible form performs the function of being the object;
and light performs the function of illumination.
Space performs the function of non-obstruction;
the mental attention arising from that performs the function of attending.
In the absence of these conditions, visual consciousness does not arise.

When the internal sense-base of the eye is unimpaired, and likewise when visible form, light, space, and the attention arising from them are unimpaired, then, through the conjunction of all these factors, the arising of visual consciousness occurs.
In that regard, it does not occur to the eye: "I perform the function of being the basis for visual consciousness.
Nor does it occur to the visible form: "I perform the function of being the object of apprehension for visual consciousness.
Nor does it occur to the light: "I perform the function of illumination for visual consciousness."
It does not occur to space: "I perform the function of non-obstruction for visual consciousness.
Nor does it occur to the attention arising therefrom: "I perform the function of directing toward for visual consciousness.
Nor does it occur to visual consciousness: "I am produced by the coming together of these conditions."
And yet, when the conditions are present, the arising and manifestation of visual consciousness occurs;
the same should be applied accordingly to the remaining sense faculties.
In that dependent origination, no dharma whatsoever transmigrates from this world to another world (thus is the negation of the extreme of eternalism),
yet there is the discernment of the fruit of karma because of the non-deficiency of causes and conditions.
(As before) / Just as fire does not burn due to a deficiency of fuel, but burns when there is no deficiency of fuel, so too...

In the very same way, the seed of consciousness, produced by karma and afflictions, brings forth the sprout of name-and-form in the mother’s womb at the moment of rebirth in various realms of existence;
this occurs within phenomena that are ownerless, unappropriated, without adversary, equal to space, and characterized by the nature of an illusion,
due to the non-deficiency of causes and conditions.
In this way, the conditional dependence of internal dependent origination is to be understood.
In this regard, internal dependent origination is to be viewed through five reasons.
What are these five?
Namely: it is not eternal;
Not through annihilation,
not through transmigration,
but through the production of a vast fruit from a small cause.
And because of its connection with what is similar to it.
How is it not eternal?
Because the final aggregates at death are different [from those that preceded them].
Other aggregates belonging to the state of rebirth appear;
however, it is not the case that those very same aggregates which belong to the end of death are the ones that appear as the aggregates belonging to the state of rebirth.
Therefore, for this reason, it is not eternal.
How, then, is it not from annihilation?
The aggregates belonging to the stage of rebirth do not manifest when the aggregates at the end of death have already ceased, nor do they manifest when those aggregates have not yet ceased.
Rather, at that very moment the aggregates of the time of death cease, and the aggregates of rebirth arise and manifest.
Like the rising and falling of the arms of a balance scale;
therefore, it is not through annihilation.
How is it not by way of transmigration?
Because from a dissimilar class of beings, dissimilar aggregates are produced in other births;
therefore, it is not by way of transmigration.
How is it that from a small cause there is the production of a vast fruit?
A small action is performed,
yet a vast ripening of fruit is experienced.
Therefore, from a small cause, there arises a vast fruit.
How is it by way of a continuous succession of similar [moments]? Just as the karma to be experienced is performed,
so too is the maturation to be experienced experienced.
Therefore, it is because of the continuous succession of similar [moments].

Venerable Śāradvatīputra, whoever perceives this dependent origination—perfectly formulated by the Blessed One, the Tathāgata—with right wisdom as it truly is: as always and constantly devoid of a soul (*ajīva*), devoid of a living being (*nirjīva*), as it really is, non-perverted, unborn, unbecome, unmade, unconditioned, immeasurable, unobstructed, auspicious, fearless, unassailable, imperishable, and having the nature of non-cessation; [that person...]
He contemplates it as unreal, as unattached, as coreless, as a disease, as a boil, as a thorn, as impermanent, as suffering, as empty, and as non-self;
he does not pursue the past, wondering: "Did I exist in the past? Or did I not exist in the past? Who indeed was I in the past?"
Or again, one does not turn back toward the future limit, thinking: "Shall I exist in the future time?
Or shall I not exist in the future time?
Who indeed shall I become?"
Nor does one pursue the present, thinking: "What indeed is this? How indeed is this?
Who are we now? What shall we become?"
It is also said in the *Āryadaśabhūmika*: "In that regard, ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*) constitute the delimitation of the path of afflictions (*kleśavartman*);

formative forces (*saṃskāra*) and existence (*bhava*) constitute the delimitation of the path of karma (*karmavartman*); and the remainder constitutes the delimitation of the path of suffering (*duḥkhavartman*)."
"Conditioned by ignorance are the formative forces"— this is the dependence on the past;
"from consciousness up to feeling"— this is the dependence on the present.
From craving up to existence— this is the expectation regarding the future limit (*aparāntika*), namely that its activity proceeds beyond this point. *Peyālam* (and so forth).
It occurs to him thus: "Through conjunction, the conditioned proceeds; through disjunction, it does not proceed."
The conditioned arises through a causal complex; it does not arise in the absence of a causal complex.
Well then, having understood that the conditioned is thus corrupted by many faults, we shall effect the cessation of this conjunction and of this causal complex.
"And yet, we shall not attain the ultimate cessation of all conditioned phenomena, for the sake of maturing sentient beings."
This is, in brief, the purification of delusion.
Reality is the syllable of the lower conventional truth, the knowledge that all phenomena, by their very nature as conventionalities, are unproduced.
Regarding this, it is said: form is of two kinds—by way of color and by way of shape.
And these are of twenty kinds: therein, blue and so forth are nine, while long and so forth are eleven.
The proposition is that all this form does not exist ultimately;
the reason is its own nature (*svarūpa*);
for it was produced by its own causes exactly as it is, yet [in reality] it is not ultimately real.
The example is "like the moon in water.
The intention of the statement "form does not exist by way of its own nature" is that "form does not exist by way of another's nature."
"Is it by way of its own nature, or by way of both natures, or by way of neither nature?"—thus says the scripture.
Conceptual construction is the category of the productive cause.
“It is neither existent, nor non-existent, nor both existent and non-existent, nor even of the nature of neither.
Such is the scripture.
The position of the agent is a conceptual construction;
regarding that, there is an illustration by way of negation:
“It is neither existent, nor non-existent, nor both existent and non-existent, nor even of the nature of neither.”
The Madhyamikas know reality to be free from the four extremes.
“Never, anywhere, are any entities ever seen to have arisen from themselves, nor from another, nor from both, nor without a cause.”

In that regard, since it is illogical for that which already exists to arise, if an existing thing were to arise, there would be an infinite regress due to the consequence of its birth being without limit.

If you argue that it is "non-existent" prior to the cause because otherwise there would be the consequence of the arising of things such as a rabbit's horn, then that very point must be examined: does the effect arise from the cause as something existent or as something non-existent?
In the arising of that which possesses both natures, how could there be the admission of two contradictory properties having a single intrinsic nature?
Let it be that the nature bound by contradictory properties is caused by an extrinsic form;
and that extrinsic form is the cultivation of those contradictory properties.
And that [cognition] is the differentiator.
In a case where there is cognition of another [object], is it not the case that there is no cognition of its own nature at all?
There is indeed cognition.
If it is argued that there is no apprehension of its own nature, and that this very [non-apprehension] is the apprehension,
then non-apprehension itself would be apprehension.
What shall we say? Now, if you claim that the absence of a cloth exists in a jar—
meaning "the jar is not a cloth"— then even the cognition of their mixture would not exist.
Therefore, the jar consists of both existence and non-existence;
hence, its dual nature is established.
True.

If, having abandoned the state of being a single body with that which is to be conventionally designated, the non-existence of form were to possess some form of its own, then— since the nature of the absence of both [form and its designation] would be perceived there as the only possible recourse— one would conventionally designate it as "the non-existence of the jar.
Therefore, there is no arising of that which possesses a dual nature.
If everything were produced without a cause, it would arise from everything;
furthermore, if the word "cause" does not refer to a single, permanent cause, then upon its production, there would always be both arising and passing away.
Because dependence arising from a single eternal cause is untenable;
if there is dependence on another, that [other] is also impermanent,
and regarding the alternative of [the cause being] impermanent, everything previously stated applies.
Therefore, does it arise from itself or from another?
Not the first, because that which has not yet arisen cannot arise by itself.
Is it by means of an unarisen form or an arisen one?
By means of an unarisen form, that which is unarisen is indeed produced,
because production is impossible through a form that is itself unarisen.
Now, as for prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), which is denoted by the term "unproduced":
does that prior non-existence arise in its own form?
If this were so, then non-being would be being.
If it is argued that [the effect] exists subsequently, then in that case, does non-existence itself become existence?
This being so, we perceive no purpose in the repeated arising of non-existence.
Furthermore, if arising were by way of another's form, it would necessarily be accepted as an arising that was previously non-existent;
yet this is not the established tenet.

Moreover, if there were arising through what has already arisen, it would follow that there is no cessation of arising within the cycles of existence, and there would be a lack of purpose [for such arising].
The second [alternative] is also not [tenable], because one thing arises from something else;
or rather, it arises by itself in another form.
There is a contradiction regarding causal activity within itself, because action is contradictory within itself;
nor is there arising from another.
How could there be production there, whether for that which is already established or for that which is not yet established?
The answer to this has already been stated: what is the use of producing that which is already established, and for that which is not yet established, there is no production at all.
By such statements as these, those [objections] that apply individually to both positions are also refuted by the principle: "If both exist, why does it not occur?"
Nor does it arise without a cause, because that would entail the consequence of everything arising everywhere and at all times, as well as the consequence of non-arising altogether.
Why is this so? From this means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*):
namely, that which is independent is not occasional, just as other causal complexes (*sāmagrī*) are.
And independence is the subject of dispute.
Therefore, being occasional is pervaded by dependence;
for whatever is occasional is dependent.
For example, a seed enclosed at the bottom of a granary with respect to the production of a sprout; and likewise, entities that occur only occasionally—
this is the point of contention.
That which is dependent is dependently originated,
just like that very seed;
and dependent entities constitute the subject of dispute.
That which has arisen dependently has not arisen by way of its own-being (*svabhāva*),
just as the moon in water arises dependently;
and dependent phenomena (*paratantra-bhāva*) are the subject of dispute.
In the *Āryacandrapradīpasūtra*: "That which is born from conditions is indeed unborn; for it has no arising by way of intrinsic nature."
That which is dependent on conditions is said to be empty;
he who understands emptiness is heedful.
Thus this statement should be held and attended to in every way, at all times, by those who see all.
(The Madhyamaka Śālistamba Sūtra is completed.)
